title: ABBA
text: This is a studio pop record built on a rock band core — electric guitars from several players, bass, drums, and Benny Andersson's piano, clavinet and synthesizer — with the keyboards often as prominent as the guitars. Over that band sit layered group vocals and dense, glassy overdubbing, so the sound is bright and worked-over rather than live-in-a-room. Side one opens with "Mamma Mia", the one track carrying a separate string arrangement, and runs mostly up-tempo and major-key through "Hey, Hey Helen", "Tropical Loveland" and "Bang-A-Boomerang", with "SOS" sitting among them as the minor-key, aching one. "Man In The Middle" is the one place on side one where a tenor saxophone is arranged in, giving that track a funkier, hornier edge than its neighbours. Side two opens on a different register: "I Do, I Do, I Do, I Do, I Do" leads with alto saxophone and old-fashioned, waltzing schmaltz, and "Rock Me" follows with the guitars pushed forward. The run of songs on side two is broken by "Intermezzo No. 1", an instrumental featuring Benny Andersson with arranged horns and strings, which is the one stretch of the record with no singing at all. Side two then closes with "I've Been Waiting For You" and "So Long", the latter driven hard and topped with a trumpet, so the record ends loud rather than fading out. It rewards attention for the vocal arrangements and the oddities — a mock-Western, a lullaby, a folk-rock tune — but the hooks are strong enough that it also works as bright background for a kitchen or a party.

title: The Best Of The Blues Project
text: This is a compilation LP drawn from an electric blues band's earlier recordings, so it plays as a sequence of separate performances rather than a single session, with shifts in recorded sound and producer from track to track. The core sound is electric guitar — wiry and a little abrasive — set against organ, with a rhythm section that swings rather than stomps, and flute arriving on at least one piece from a jazzier direction. Side one opens with a fast Chuck Berry cover, "I Want To Be Your Driver", drops into Steve Katz's own "Steve's Song", which is the gentler, folk-leaning moment of the side, and ends with "Wake Me, Shake Me", an arrangement by Al Kooper that drives hard and long. Side two is the longer and more varied side: it begins with the Blind Willie Johnson blues "I Can't Keep From Crying Sometimes" stretched well past its original shape into modal, raga-tinged jamming, then lightens into the pop-folk of Bob Lind's "Cheryl's Going Home". Also on side two, "The Flute Thing" is the instrumental, with flute improvising over organ and bass in a jazz manner, before Eric Andersen's "Violets Of Dawn" slows things to a sung folk ballad and the side closes with Kooper's "No Time Like The Right Time", a brisk, hook-led piece. Across both sides the density changes a lot, from loose two- or three-minute band songs to extended group improvisation, so the record rewards attention more than it sits quietly behind conversation. It suits someone who wants the point where coffeehouse folk material — Lind, Andersen, Katz — was being played loud by a blues-rock band with an organ, and who doesn't mind a compilation's uneven flow. Because the covers and originals alternate rather than group together, neither side settles into one mood for long, and the quieter songs function as breathing space between the long workouts.

title: Never Too Much
text: The band across the record is a tight rhythm section of electric bass, drums, keyboards and guitar, thickened with congas and hand percussion on almost every track. Side one is the busier side: its first two tracks add strings and horns over the rhythm section and carry a large group of backing singers, so the sound is dense and layered rather than spare. The opening title track is up-tempo and built for movement, with the bass line and the massed voices driving it rather than any loud peak in the singing. Midway through side one the arrangements thin out — "Don't You Know That?" drops the horns and keeps strings over a smaller vocal group, and "I've Been Working" runs on rhythm section, synthesizer and voices with no strings at all. Side two opens with its fullest arrangement, strings, horns, two percussionists and a six-voice choir on "She's A Super Lady", then pares back to rhythm section and strings for "You Stopped Loving Me". Side two ends slowest, with the Bacharach and David ballad "A House Is Not A Home" sung over keyboards, two basses and strings and horns, and no backing vocals credited at all, which leaves the lead voice exposed and unhurried. Taken as a whole the record moves from dance-floor momentum at the start of side one to a long closing ballad, so it suits late-evening listening that can begin as background and end wanting your attention. Nothing here is abrasive or loud-dynamic; the force comes from the thickness of the stacked vocal harmonies and the bass, not from volume.

title: Believer
text: Smerz's "Believer" is built by the duo themselves — Catharina Stoltenberg and Henriette Motzfeldt write, produce, engineer and perform all of it — so the voices and the programming sit very close together, with no session band between them. Acoustic strings and flute run through the record as a real, played presence rather than samples: cello, two violins and flute are credited, and they appear as small chamber figures, not as a full orchestral bed. Against that, the rhythm side of the record is sparse electronic programming with sub-bass, often leaving long gaps where a beat would normally carry on. The vocals are close-mic'd and half-spoken, deadpan one moment and plainly sincere the next, which is what the record asks you to follow rather than any melodic hook. Side one is the shorter and more composed half, moving from guitar figure to the title track and on through "Versace Strings" and "4 Temaer" before ending on "Hester, Pt. 1", so it plays as a handful of pieces given room. Side two picks up directly with "Hester, Pt. 2" and then fragments into many short pieces — interludes, an untitled closer, titles like "Rap Interlude" and "Grand Piano" — so it moves faster and breaks off more often, with tracks stopping mid-thought instead of resolving. Three side-one tracks carry additional production or mixing from Peder Mannerfelt, and those are the harder-edged, more processed moments on that side. It suits low-volume listening alone or late in an evening and rewards attention — the silences and the abrupt endings are the point — but it is too quiet and too interrupted to work as a steady background for conversation.
